overview: This file concerns postwar aviation policy in U.S.-occupied East Asia in 1948. An April telegram recommends against granting a French civil-air franchise in southern Korea because Gimpo’s facilities were inadequate and existing American carriers deserved priority. The remainder documents the State and War Departments’ response to Soviet questions in the Far Eastern Commission about the expensive reconstruction of Misawa Airfield: officials justified it as necessary for occupation aircraft, border-control operations, emergency landings, and eventual commercial aviation, while recommending that the United States not volunteer an explanation unless pressed.

subfiles.title: CINCFE telegram opposing a French civil-air franchise in Korea
subfiles.from: Commander in Chief, Far East (CINCFE), Tokyo
subfiles.to: Department of the Army; information to CG USAFIK, CG FEAF, and Department of State
subfiles.about: Recommends rejecting any French request for a civil-air franchise in Korea because Gimpo could not support more traffic.
subfiles.summary: CINCFE opposes a French civil-air franchise in Korea, citing Kimpo's limited capacity and favoring Northwest and INAC for any priority.

subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP concerning Soviet questions about Misawa Airfield
subfiles.from: George C. Marshall, Department of State
subfiles.to: Acting Political Adviser, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo; information to Army Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Alerts SCAP that Soviet questions about the purpose, cost, and post-treaty fate of Misawa Airfield might be raised again.
subfiles.summary: A Soviet FEC Steering Committee member cites a Times article on a $13 million Misawa field for heavy bombers, asking why it's needed near occupation's end and its postwar fate; State consults the Air Force on responding.

subfiles.title: War Department explanation of the improvement of Misawa Airfield
subfiles.from: Major General Daniel Noce, Chief, Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.to: P. P. Claxton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains the military and civil-aviation reasons for reconstructing Misawa and other Japanese airfields.
subfiles.summary: War Department explains Misawa's May 1946 upgrade addressed Japan's runways being too weak for American aircraft, serving occupation, anti-smuggling, and emergency needs; facilities would revert to Japan postwar unless treaty-barred.

subfiles.title: Claxton cover memorandum on the Misawa inquiry
subfiles.about: Reports Claxton’s discussion with General Noce and forwards a copy of the memorandum requesting information about Misawa.
subfiles.summary: Claxton reports discussing Misawa with General Noce, who requested and received a written memorandum, copied to Saltzman.

subfiles.title: Claxton memorandum requesting an investigation of Misawa Airfield
subfiles.from: P. P. Claxton Jr., Department of State
subfiles.to: Major General Daniel Noce, Chief, Civil Affairs Division, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: Requests exact information with which to answer anticipated Far Eastern Commission criticism of Misawa and similar airfields.
subfiles.summary: Claxton recounts Soviet questions about Misawa, suggests defending it only as an occupation necessity, and requests a full investigation of its construction and purpose.

subfiles.title: Draft guidance to the U.S. member of the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.to: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Advises the U.S. member not to volunteer an answer about Misawa but authorizes use of an attached statement if the issue is raised again.
subfiles.summary: Draft guidance says the U.S. FEC member never agreed to supply Misawa information and should not volunteer it, but may use the enclosed statement if pressed again.

subfiles.title: Proposed statement defending Misawa Airfield improvements
subfiles.from: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission, as drafted by the Department of State
subfiles.to: Members of the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Provides a prepared explanation that Misawa was improved to make the occupation effective and aviation safer.
subfiles.summary: Statement defends Misawa's 1946 upgrade as addressing weak Japanese runways for occupation, anti-smuggling, and emergency needs, improving safety for military and approved commercial use.

interest: Shows Soviet scrutiny of Misawa Airfield's wartime-scale construction near occupation's end, and Korean airline-franchise competition.
